item.title: The World Economy Is Swerving, and the Destination Is Unknown
item.description: The days of unfettered globalization, multilateral rule of law, commonly accepted limits on economic statecraft, and widely shared macroeconomic objectives are now long gone. A perpetual, directionless transition is our new reality, and corporate executives, investors, and policymakers must adapt accordingly.

item.title: Is China Really a Beggar-thy-Neighbor Power?
item.description: When major economies are running at near full capacity, it is not clear that trade deficits should be a cause for concern, since they represent a transfer of purchasing power from surplus countries. Under the current circumstances, then, China’s widely criticized surpluses might as well be called enrich-thy-neighbor.

item.title: No Escape from the Russian Terror Playbook
item.description: When Vladimir Putin revives Stalin-era repression tactics, he does not do so in service of some lofty ideology or grand project. Rather, he and his security apparatus are seeking to safeguard their own power indefinitely—and, as Russians well know, they will stop at nothing to succeed.

item.title: The Extractive Trap Has a Green Exit
item.description: For resource-rich developing countries, decades of resource extraction have produced income concentration, economic dependency, external vulnerabilities, and the weakening of other productive sectors. Achieving broad-based prosperity requires a new approach, one which leverages South-South cooperation to build green industries.

item.title: The Last Trump Election
item.description: No matter what US President Donald Trump says or does in response to the results of this November’s midterms, he will have faced his final popular vote. There will be further damage done to public confidence in American democratic institutions, but the institutions themselves will hold.

item.title: The Ceuta Crisis Is About More Than Migration
item.description: When tens of thousands of people recently entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from neighboring Morocco, European leaders lapsed into recriminations, reigniting the debate on migration. But the bigger challenge is to address a long-simmering territorial dispute between Spain and Morocco.

item.title: The Rising Price of a Cheap Renminbi
item.description: Renminbi appreciation would not, on its own, rebalance China’s economy and eliminate its massive surpluses. But by increasing households’ purchasing power over imports and compressing tradable-sector margins, it would raise the cost of avoiding reform.

item.title: Who Should Build the Low-Carbon Economy?
item.description: Since the first Industrial Revolution, goods and technologies have reached the farthest corners of the world, but the ability to design, build, market, and extract value from them has remained highly concentrated. Unless humanity can break this pattern, a sufficient response to climate change will remain out of reach.

item.title: Will Iceland Rejoin the EU Path?
item.description: US President Donald Trump’s volatile and unpredictable security policies, particularly his desire to control Greenland, have put Iceland in a vulnerable position. This uncomfortable reality will likely be front of mind as voters decide whether to reopen membership negotiations with the European Union.

item.title: Democracy, Autocracy, or Something Else?
item.description: Contrary to conventional wisdom, the world is neither converging on liberal democracy nor being swept by an authoritarian tide. The decisive political struggles of the 21st century will be won or lost through the unglamorous work of strengthening democratic accountability and building effective institutions.

item.title: Colombia’s New Right-Wing Government Faces an Uphill Battle
item.description: Colombian President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella inherits an economy constrained by weak investment and a severe fiscal crisis. His ability to restore fiscal stability without sacrificing the social gains of recent decades will determine whether the country’s rightward shift proves lasting or short-lived.

item.title: Can Progressives Deliver Economic Growth?
item.description: At a time of historic inequality and inadequate public investment, the kind of redistributive policies promoted by politicians on the left are badly needed. But given that no jurisdiction can tax and regulate its way to affordability, a growth-enhancing agenda that generates good jobs and productive capacity is also vital.

item.title: Fauci’s Modern Pillory
item.description: MAGA Republicans’ decision to drag Anthony Fauci before a Senate hearing was less about their hatred of science and more about their disdain for the scientists who guide lawmakers in their decision-making. They couldn’t wait to pillory him, and by association any public-facing expert, in front of the cameras.

item.title: Cheaper Mortgages Won’t Solve the US Housing Crisis
item.description: For decades, federal housing policy has favored cheaper financing over expanding the housing supply, despite evidence that expanding mortgage credit increases borrowing and house prices. The bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act marks an important shift by emphasizing measures that make it easier to build more homes.

item.title: The Right Way to Regulate AI
item.description: Governments tend to treat AI as a national-security challenge while devoting far less attention to its effects on education, health, labor markets, and the judiciary. Addressing AI’s societal risks requires institutions designed to recognize and respond to emerging threats before they become systemic failures.

item.title: Global Tax Reform Is the Key to a Fair AI Economy
item.description: The rise of AI has highlighted how the global tax system is ill-suited to capture the profits derived from such technology. While creating an equitable AI economy ultimately requires a durable and robust multilateral tax framework, digital-service taxes can serve as an important stepping stone to that outcome.

item.title: Aid’s Next Chapter
item.description: Wars, epidemics, displacement, and geopolitical competition will ensure that rich countries continue to spend money abroad, whether for humanitarian reasons or in pursuit of their own interests. The only question is what sort of aid system will emerge from the current retrenchment.

item.title: Peace With Iran Won’t Last Unless It Benefits Ordinary Iranians
item.description: A sustainable peace agreement between the United States and Iran will require more than military deterrence. Without financial sanctions relief that fuels job creation and generates real economic opportunities for ordinary Iranians, it will likely suffer the same fate as the 2015 nuclear deal.

item.title: Why Wealth Taxes Always Fail
item.description: A clear-eyed view of past experience shows that where wealth taxes have been tried, they have usually been abandoned—and for good reason. As policymakers in California, New York, France, and elsewhere revisit this old idea, they should heed the lessons of this history.

item.title: A New Paradigm for Global Health Financing
item.description: As aid flows decline, more countries are articulating a new vision in which health financing would build on national resources, answer to domestic priorities, and remain accountable to their own citizens. Such a change is long overdue, and it can be achieved by pursuing reforms in three areas.
